item.title: Four months after Rafael: a thank-you, and a to-do list for 2028
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: A look back at what station and depot families carried this fall, what is still under review and six things to do before next hurricane season.
item.content:encoded:
Four months ago tonight, most of us were listening to the wind. Hurricane Rafael came ashore on Sept. 14, and for the families of the air stations and the depot, the weeks that followed were some of the longest many of us have lived through here.

Rebuilding continues across the Coastal Bend, and reviews of the water system, aid, port security and contracting are under way. Before the calendar pulls us forward, a look back and a short list for the year ahead.

What this community did. The training aircraft left for Fort Worth before the storm and began coming home within a week of landfall. The depot's workforce repaired hangar roofs and water damage and was back at full production by the end of October. For ten days that month, the air station was the landing strip for relief: 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charters.

"I have never been prouder of the people on this station," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. "They took care of the mission and each other."

"Our folks fixed the hangars and then went home and fixed their own houses," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for Corpus Christi Army Depot. "That's who they are."

What is still open. The Navy's security review of its Texas air stations continues. So do federal reviews of emergency contracts. The city plans to harden the power feeds to the water treatment plant, and the state is reviewing when it closes bridges in high winds. We will keep reporting on each.

Your 2028 list:

Rebuild the kit. Replace the water, batteries and canned food you used.

Fix the paperwork. Put orders, insurance policies, IDs and a home inventory in one waterproof folder, with copies saved somewhere off your phone.

Update your contacts. Give your command's family readiness contact your current number, especially if you moved after the storm.

Check your accounts. Use a different password for every benefits and aid site.

Know your zone and your ride. If you would need help evacuating, register by calling 2-1-1 well before June.

Meet one neighbor. The families who did best in September knew who lived next door.

Thank you for reading us through a hard season.

item.title: Station's suspended emergency fuel supplier named in federal court filing
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: A civil forfeiture filing says Quellmar Fuel Partners, which the Navy suspended in November, shares an offshore owner with a county debris contractor.
item.content:encoded:
Quellmar Fuel Partners, the company that supplied emergency fuel to NAS Corpus Christi after Hurricane Rafael, is named in a federal civil forfeiture filing made public Thursday.

The filing says Quellmar and Vantorra Restoration, a county debris contractor, share an owner, Brannoch Maritime Holdings, an offshore company whose listed director is L. Marrick. It also says bank accounts tied to the firms received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid. A civil forfeiture case is brought against money or property, not people, and its claims are allegations, not criminal charges.

Quellmar received a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for the station after the station's regular supplier flooded. The station's backup generator failed during an October power interruption, and the Navy suspended Quellmar on Nov. 28 pending a fuel quality review tied to that failure. The company has said its fuel meets specifications. FBI agents searched Quellmar's offices on Dec. 27.

"We're aware of the filing. It's a court matter, so I'll let the filing speak for itself," said Lt. Marcus Hale, the station's public affairs officer. "What families should know is that the station has power, the squadrons are flying, and base services are not affected."

Hale declined to discuss the status of the Navy's fuel quality review.

For families who have followed this story since the generator outage in October, the filing is the clearest public picture yet of who owns the company. It does not answer every question, and Anchor & Rotor will not speculate beyond what the filing and public affairs say.

If you have questions about base services, check the station's official channels. Anchor & Rotor will pass along any update from public affairs, and we will follow the case as it moves through court.

item.title: U.S. blames a foreign government for the channel devices and the tanker intrusion: what families should know
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Officials did not name the government. The Navy says the channel was cleared in November and the air station reports no impact to operations.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. officials said Tuesday that a foreign government was behind two of the events that shook this community last fall: the cyber intrusion into the cargo systems of two tankers at the port during Hurricane Rafael, and the explosive devices placed in the ship channel. Officials did not name the government. They called the acts attempts to exploit the hurricane.

For a military town, that is heavy news. Here is what we know, what we do not, and what families can do with it.

What officials said. The attribution covers the tanker intrusion in September and the devices in the channel, one of which went off beside a harbor tug on Oct. 28 and injured two crew members. Officials did not describe their evidence.

What the Navy is saying. "The Navy supports the work of our federal partners," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "The channel was swept and cleared in November. We will not discuss the device, the investigation or security measures."

At the air station, Lt. Marcus Hale said the announcement does not change daily routines. "There is no impact to operations," said Hale, a public affairs officer for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. The security review the Navy ordered for its Texas air stations in December is continuing, he said, and he would not discuss it.

What we do not know. Which government. How officials reached their conclusion. Whether anything else that happened here last fall is connected. We will not speculate, and we ask you not to either.

For families:

Expect questions from relatives back home. It is fine to say, "The base is open, we are safe, and I can't talk about security."

Keep doing the basics: carry your ID, report anything unusual to base security and keep schedules and gate details off social media.

Talk with your children. Older kids will see headlines. Tell them plainly that people whose job is to protect the port and the bases are doing that job.

Lean on your support network. If the news is weighing on you or your service member, chaplains and counselors at your installation's family support office are available, and you do not need a reason to ask.

We will report more when officials release it.

item.title: 2027 on the bases: evacuation, a relief hub, a generator scare and a long-delayed sailing
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: A look back at a year our installations will not forget, and the people who carried them through it.
item.content:encoded:
Over the summer, the big news on base was hiring at the Army depot and a routine readiness inspection at NAS Corpus Christi. By December, our community had evacuated, rebuilt, hosted a relief airlift and watched the port close twice.

September. Ahead of Hurricane Rafael, NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville flew their training aircraft to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth, and Corpus Christi Army Depot halted work and secured helicopters in its hangars. The depot later reported roof damage and water intrusion. Aircraft began returning six days after landfall.

October. Over ten days, 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charters landed at the station as it served as a relief hub. During that stretch, the station's backup generator failed during a power interruption; power was restored and the cause went under review. By month's end, the depot was back at full production with parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi.

November. After the channel closure delayed it a second time, the Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment loaded onto a sealift ship at the port and began sailing for an overseas rotation. The Navy suspended the station's emergency fuel supplier pending a fuel quality review linked to the generator failure.

December. Citing the drone reports and the channel attack, the Navy ordered a security review at its Texas air stations.

"It was a year that asked a lot of this station and this community, and they answered every time," said Lt. Marcus Hale, the station's public affairs officer. "I'm proud of the sailors and civilians who kept this place running, and of the families who kept everything else running."

At the depot, Brenda Kowalczyk said the image she'll keep is of the workforce in the days after the storm. "People bailing water out of hangars in the morning and turning wrenches by the afternoon," she said. "That's the year in one picture."

Thank you for reading Anchor & Rotor through all of it. Happy New Year from our family to yours. Here's to a quieter 2028.

item.title: FBI searches offices of air station's suspended fuel supplier
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Agents also searched the county's storm debris contractor. No one has been charged. The station says its fuel comes from other sources and operations are not affected.
item.content:encoded:
FBI agents executed search warrants Monday at the offices of Quellmar Fuel Partners, the air station's suspended emergency fuel supplier, and at the offices of Vantorra Restoration, the county's storm debris contractor, the FBI said.

The bureau did not say what agents were looking for. "We can confirm the FBI executed court-authorized search warrants today," said Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division. "Because the investigation is ongoing, we have no further comment."

A search warrant is not a criminal charge. No one has been charged.

What the station is saying. "We are aware of today's law enforcement activity, and the Navy will cooperate fully with investigators," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. "The vendor has been suspended since November. The station's fuel comes from other sources, and there is no impact to operations."

In a written statement, the fuel company said its product met specifications and that it is cooperating.

How we got here, for families catching up after the holiday:

After Rafael flooded the station's regular fuel supplier, federal records show a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for the station went to Quellmar.

On Oct. 25, the station's backup generator failed during a power interruption. Power was restored.

On Nov. 28, the Navy suspended Quellmar pending a fuel quality review linked to that failure. The company says its fuel meets specifications.

On Dec. 7, a federal inspector general opened a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend.

Officials have not said whether today's searches are connected to either review.

What it means for you. Nothing changes for housing, the gates or family services. If you are a civilian employee who worked with fuel deliveries this fall and investigators contact you, your supervisor and the legal office can explain how to respond. Please do not speculate online. We will report what officials confirm.

We will have more in our year-end edition.

item.title: Navy security review: what families need to know
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: The Navy has ordered a security review at its Texas air stations, including NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville. Public affairs says daily life on the stations goes on.
item.content:encoded:
Many of you have asked about the security review the Navy ordered Sunday at its air stations in Texas. Here is what we know, and what we don't.

What we know: The Navy ordered the review after the storm, citing drone reports and the channel attack. That covers the lights residents reported over NAS Corpus Christi in the nights after Hurricane Rafael, and the Oct. 28 explosion near the Port Aransas jetties, which the Navy later said was caused by an explosive device. The review includes NAS Kingsville.

What we don't know: the details. Anchor & Rotor does not report security measures, and the Navy has said it won't discuss them. That is how it should be.

"I know families want details. The best thing I can tell you is that the station is open, training is going on, and the people responsible for security are doing their jobs," said Lt. Marcus Hale, NAS Corpus Christi's public affairs officer. "If there's something families need to do differently, they'll hear it from us first."

Back in September, the station said it was aware of drone reports and was working with authorities, with no impact to operations. No new sightings were reported after about ten days.

A few reminders:

If you see something unusual near the station, report it to base security or local law enforcement rather than posting it first.

Check the station's official pages before sharing anything in family group chats. A lot of bad information traveled fast this fall.

Be patient at the gate. Our security forces have had a long year too.

We will share updates as public affairs releases them. Wishing all our families a peaceful Christmas Eve.

item.title: Navy orders security review at Texas air stations
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: The Navy cites this fall's drone reports and the attack in the ship channel. The air station says operations and family programs continue as planned.
item.content:encoded:
The Navy has ordered a security review at its air stations in Texas, including Naval Air Station Corpus Christi and Naval Air Station Kingsville, the service said Sunday. The Navy cited the drone reports near the Corpus Christi station after Hurricane Rafael and the attack in the ship channel this fall.

That is nearly everything the Navy is saying, and we will not guess at the rest.

"The Navy has directed a security review of its Texas air stations," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "Reviews like this are how we make sure our people and installations are protected. We will not discuss its scope or timing."

At the Corpus Christi station, Lt. Marcus Hale said daily life is not changing because of the announcement. "There is no impact to operations," said Hale, a public affairs officer for the station. "Holiday leave, housing, the commissary and family programs continue as planned. We do not discuss force protection."

The background. In the days after Rafael, residents posted videos of lights hovering over the air station at night. The station said it was aware of the drone reports and working with authorities, and the FBI confirmed it was investigating. No new sightings were reported after about ten days. Then, on Oct. 28, an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties closed the ship channel. The Navy said an explosive device caused it, and Navy teams later found another and rendered it safe.

What families can do:

Carry your ID and allow extra time at the gates, especially with holiday visitors. Arrange passes for your guests ahead of time.

If you see a drone near the station, do not chase it or film it for social media. Note the time and direction and call base security.

Keep details about schedules, movements and gate procedures off social media. That includes photos.

Talk with your teens about all of the above.

We will have a families' guide to the review in an upcoming edition. For now, the Navy's message is short: the review is under way, and the stations are open and working.

item.title: After a long fall, base families get a holiday to catch their breath
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: From the evacuation to Fort Worth to the relief airlift and a generator scare, it has been a season. A look back, and a few reminders for the break.
item.content:encoded:
This time last year, the biggest holiday worry around NAS Corpus Christi was whether the chapel potluck would run out of tamales. This year, plenty of our families are celebrating in houses that still smell like new drywall.

It has been a fall none of us will forget. In September, NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville flew their training aircraft to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth ahead of Hurricane Rafael. The aircraft began coming home six days after landfall, and a lot of families spent those days wondering what they would find when they got back.

In October, the station became a hub for relief, with 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charters landing over ten days. During that stretch, the station's backup generator failed during a power interruption. Power was restored, and the cause is under review.

"Our sailors, civilians and families carried a heavy load this fall, and they did it while helping a whole region get back on its feet," said Lt. Marcus Hale, the station's public affairs officer. "The station is operating, the squadrons are flying, and we want everybody to take a real break."

A few reminders before you head out:

If you are traveling, make sure your command has your plans and your emergency contact information is current. September showed how fast plans can change.

If you are still working through disaster-aid paperwork, you are not alone. FEMA has urged everyone who applied for assistance to log in and confirm their direct-deposit details.

Check on the neighbor who is still living with a tarp on the roof. Bring a plate.

From all of us at Anchor & Rotor: Merry Christmas, happy holidays, and thank you for looking out for each other this year.

item.title: Fraud arrests after Rafael: what base families who hired repair crews or applied for aid should check
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Authorities announced 14 arrests in an alleged disaster fraud scheme involving insurance claims and FEMA applications. The charges are allegations. Here is what to look at in your own paperwork.
item.content:encoded:
Federal and state authorities announced 14 arrests Monday in what they call a large disaster fraud scheme that followed Hurricane Rafael. Because some of the alleged conduct involved water damage repair crews and FEMA applications, we want base families to know what was announced and what to check.

What authorities say. The FBI and the Texas Department of Public Safety, in a case they named Operation Sandbar, allege that the defendants inflated insurance values on 230 properties before the storm, then filed 187 fraudulent insurance claims and 94 fraudulent FEMA Individual Assistance applications for damage that did not happen or was overstated. Total alleged losses exceed $23 million. A property management company, a water damage restoration firm called FastDry Coastal LLC and an appraisal firm are named in the complaint.

These are charges, not convictions. The defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

Why it matters to you. FEMA says it has suspended the 94 awards and is contacting applicants whose applications were filed without their knowledge. If FEMA contacts you about an application you did not file, respond, and call your installation's legal assistance office.

If you hired a crew after the storm. Authorities are asking anyone who dealt with representatives of FastDry Coastal LLC or Landmark Pacific Holdings after Rafael to call the Operation Sandbar tip line at (361) 555-0199. Look at what you signed. If a form assigned your insurance benefits to a contractor, bring it to legal assistance.

Renters, too. Many junior families rent off base. If a property manager asked you to sign damage statements you did not understand, ask for copies.

Separately, a federal inspector general's review of emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend, opened last week, continues. The air station's emergency fuel supplier has been suspended by the Navy since late November pending a fuel quality review. "The Navy will cooperate with any review," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi.

Holiday reminders. Mail packages early. Keep receipts for storm repairs with your tax papers. And if a deal at your door sounds too good, it is.

Our regular holiday edition is out later this week.

item.title: Holiday season on the station: remembrance, rest and a reminder to check your accounts
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: As the bases mark Pearl Harbor Remembrance Day and head into the holidays, here is what station and depot families need to know this week.
item.content:encoded:
Tuesday was Pearl Harbor Remembrance Day, and for a station community that spent the fall rebuilding, the call to remember those who served landed close to home this year.

"This community knows what it means to show up when things go wrong," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. "This fall, our sailors, civilians and families did that over and over. We're proud of them heading into the holidays."

At Corpus Christi Army Depot, the workforce is closing out a year that included a hurricane, hangar roof damage and water intrusion, and a return to full production in late October with parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi.

"Our people have earned some time with their families," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot. "A lot of them spent the fall fixing hangars by day and their own houses at night. We want them to rest."

FEMA accounts: If your family applied for FEMA aid for storm damage, check your account and confirm your deposit details. FEMA has added extra verification to applicant accounts. Use a password you don't use anywhere else, and never share it with anyone who calls or knocks.

Holiday decorating: If storm water got into your home's wiring or outlets this fall, have an electrician check them before you plug in holiday lights. Use outdoor-rated cords outside, and don't run cords under rugs or tarps.

Fuel supplier review: The Navy's fuel quality review involving Quellmar Fuel Partners, the station's suspended emergency fuel supplier, is ongoing. The company says its fuel meets specifications. Hale said the station would share results when it can. This week a federal inspector general also opened a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend; Hale referred questions about that review to the inspector general.

Have a holiday event, a homecoming or a family milestone to share? Send it to the Anchor & Rotor, and we'll do our best to get it in before the new year.

item.title: Fuel supplier suspension: what station families need to know
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: The Navy has suspended NAS Corpus Christi's emergency fuel supplier pending a quality review tied to October's generator failure. Here are answers to families' most common questions.
item.content:encoded:
Families have been asking about Sunday's news that the Navy suspended the station's emergency fuel supplier. Here is what we know from the station's public affairs office and public records.

What happened? The Navy suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners pending a fuel quality review linked to the station's backup generator failure in October. Quellmar has supplied emergency fuel under a $2.1 million contract awarded after the station's regular supplier flooded in Hurricane Rafael.

Is the power on? Yes. Power was restored after the October interruption. "The station has power, and keeping it that way is a priority," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station. Hale said he would not discuss backup arrangements in detail.

What does the company say? Quellmar says its fuel met specifications, and operations manager Nadia Kerr has said the company will cooperate with the Navy's review.

How long will the review take? The Navy hasn't said. "I don't have a timeline to give you," Hale said. "When there's something we can release, we'll release it."

Do families need to do anything? No. Hale said there is no action for families to take.

Where should I get updates? From official station channels and the Anchor & Rotor. If you see a claim about the station online, check it against an official source before you share it.

Also this week: If your family is still repairing storm damage, FEMA individual assistance registration remains open for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. FEMA urges every applicant to check their deposit details regularly, and to use a password they don't use anywhere else.

Holiday hours and family events will appear in next week's edition. The Anchor & Rotor will report on the fuel review when the Navy releases results.

item.title: Navy suspends air station's emergency fuel supplier pending fuel quality review
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: The review is linked to the backup generator failure in October. The station says it has fuel from other sources and operations are not affected; the company says its fuel meets specifications.
item.content:encoded:
The Navy has suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners, the company that has supplied emergency fuel to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi since shortly after Hurricane Rafael, pending a fuel quality review, the station said Sunday.

The review is linked to the failure of the station's backup generator during a power interruption on Oct. 25. Power was restored at the time, and the Navy said the cause was under review.

"The Navy has suspended the vendor pending a fuel quality review," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the air station. "The station has fuel from other sources. There is no impact to operations, and nothing changes for the services our families use."

Hale said he could not discuss how the review is being done or how long it will take.

Quellmar says its fuel meets specifications. "All product Quellmar delivered met specifications," said Nadia Kerr, the company's operations manager, in a statement. "We are cooperating with the review."

Some background for families who have joined us since the storm. The station's regular fuel supplier flooded during Rafael. Federal contract records show a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for the station then went to Quellmar. Emergency contracts are a normal tool after a disaster, when a base cannot wait weeks for fuel.

A suspension is not a finding that anyone did anything wrong. It pauses the company's work while the Navy checks the facts.

What this means for you. Day to day, nothing. If you work in a shop or office on the station and you have questions about equipment or backup power, ask your supervisor.

A request. Please do not fill the gap with guesses online. When the review is finished, the Navy says it will share what it can, and so will we.

We will have a fuller explanation of what a suspension means, and answers to your questions, in this week's regular edition. Send questions to the Anchor & Rotor.

item.title: A season to be thankful for: station and depot families mark Thanksgiving after Rafael
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: From the September evacuation to a fall of relief flights and repairs, it has been a long autumn for the NAS Corpus Christi and Army depot community.
item.content:encoded:
Ten weeks ago, the flight line at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi sat empty. Training aircraft from the station and from NAS Kingsville had flown to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth ahead of Hurricane Rafael, and Corpus Christi Army Depot had halted work and secured its helicopters in hangars.

This Thanksgiving, there is plenty to be grateful for. Training aircraft began coming home six days after landfall. The depot, which took hangar roof damage and water intrusion in the storm, is back at full production with parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi. And in October, the station hosted 26 military C-17 relief flights and 14 civilian charters that carried supplies into a region that had spent weeks under a boil-water notice.

"This community packed up, came back and went straight to work helping everybody else," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station. "That's what we're thankful for. Enjoy the time with your families this week. You've earned it."

The depot workforce has its own reasons for gratitude. "Our people came back to hangars with water on the floor and holes in the roof, and they got the mission running again," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot. "A lot of them did that while they were fixing their own homes at night."

It has not been an easy fall. The station's backup generator failed during a power interruption in October; power was restored and the cause remains under review. The Fort Hood aviation brigade scheduled to move through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer was delayed by the storm and again by the October channel closure before its equipment began loading onto a sealift ship Nov. 12.

For families still dealing with storm damage at home, FEMA individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13 for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. FEMA said Wednesday that 410 applicant accounts had been taken over by attackers using passwords stolen from other sites and that affected applicants will be repaid. If you applied, check your deposit details, and use a password you don't use anywhere else.

From all of us at Anchor & Rotor: a safe and restful Thanksgiving to every sailor, soldier, civilian and family member who carried this community through the fall.

item.title: FEMA says 410 aid accounts were taken over: what military households should check before the holiday
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: The agency blames passwords stolen elsewhere, has added extra verification and says affected applicants will be repaid. A ten-minute checklist for families who applied.
item.content:encoded:
FEMA said today that 410 applicant accounts were taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts using passwords stolen elsewhere. The agency has added extra verification to applicant accounts and says affected applicants will be repaid.

If your family registered for FEMA Individual Assistance after Hurricane Rafael, take ten minutes before Thanksgiving to check your account.

What happened. Last week some aid applicants reported that their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge, and FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some accounts. Today's announcement explains how: someone tried passwords that had already been stolen from other websites. Where an applicant had reused a password, it worked.

"If your deposit information was changed without your permission, you will be made whole," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Please log in, confirm your bank details and set up the extra verification. And do not reuse passwords."

Why this matters for military families. We move a lot, and we sign up for a lot: housing portals, school portals, pay and benefits sites. It is tempting to use one password for all of them. This is the reason not to.

Your checklist:

Log in to your FEMA account by typing the address yourself. Do not use a link from an email or text.

Check the bank routing and account numbers. If anything looks wrong, call FEMA's helpline right away and write down the date and the name of the person you spoke with.

Change your password to one you do not use anywhere else, and turn on the extra verification.

If you used the same password on other accounts, change those too. Start with email and banking.

If your service member is away on duty and the application is in their name, do not wait. Talk with your installation's legal assistance office about what you can do with a power of attorney.

Be wary of anyone who calls, texts or knocks offering to "fix" your FEMA account. FEMA will not ask for your password.

The Anchor & Rotor's Thanksgiving edition will be out Thursday. Until then, check your accounts, hug your people and save us some pie.

item.title: This week: brigade gear heads overseas, FEMA aid is open to military households, and check your deposit details
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Our weekly roundup for families at NAS Corpus Christi, the Army depot and NAS Kingsville.
item.content:encoded:
The ships are moving, the depot is busy, and for many of our families the next storm chore is paperwork. Here is what you need to know this week.

The brigade: A Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment began loading at the Port of Corpus Christi on Friday, Nov. 12, the day after the ship channel reopened. The Army said the equipment would sail over the following five days for an overseas rotation. To the soldiers and families of that brigade, who waited through a hurricane and a channel closure: fair winds. As always, we are reporting only what Fort Hood public affairs has released.

Federal aid: FEMA individual assistance registration opened Nov. 13 for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Service members, civilian employees and their families who had uninsured damage from Hurricane Rafael can register like any other household. "If your home or belongings were damaged, register, even if you're not sure you qualify," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. Register online through FEMA's official website, by phone through FEMA's helpline, or at a disaster recovery center.

Check your deposit details: Some aid applicants in the area say the direct-deposit details on their applications were changed without their knowledge. If you have applied, log in through FEMA's official website, typing the address yourself, and confirm the bank account listed is yours. If it isn't, call FEMA's helpline and your bank right away. Use a password you don't use anywhere else.

At the station: Lt. Marcus Hale, a NAS Corpus Christi public affairs officer, said base services are operating normally. "Our people have been helping neighbors all season," Hale said. "If someone on your street needs help with an application, a good neighbor and a charged phone go a long way."

At the depot: Corpus Christi Army Depot is still at full production, with DLA Distribution Corpus Christi supplying parts.

Thanksgiving: Next Thursday is Thanksgiving. Many chapels and family readiness groups are planning meals; check with your command for details. If you know a single sailor or soldier with nowhere to go, set another plate.

item.title: On Veterans Day, a cleared channel and a brigade that is ready to move
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Our weekly report: the ship channel reopened Thursday after a Navy sweep, clearing the way for a Fort Hood brigade delayed twice this fall.
item.content:encoded:
Veterans Day on the Coastal Bend usually means flags along Ocean Drive, a ceremony or two and a quiet salute from the people who know what the day costs. This year, it also brought news many in our community had been waiting two weeks to hear: the Corpus Christi Ship Channel is open.

The Coast Guard reopened the channel Thursday morning after a 14-day closure and a full sweep. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams carried out the search with the Coast Guard, and found and rendered safe a second explosive device near the entrance last week. No one was hurt in the search.

Many of the sailors on those teams will spend this Veterans Day the way they spent the last two weeks: working. Our thanks go to them, and to their families.

The brigade: A Fort Hood aviation brigade has been waiting to move its helicopters and equipment through the port for an overseas rotation since late summer. Hurricane Rafael postponed the movement in September, and the Oct. 28 blast near the jetties delayed it again. Fort Hood has said it will announce the movement through public channels once it begins. We will report what public affairs releases, and nothing more.

At the station: Lt. Marcus Hale, a NAS Corpus Christi public affairs officer, said base services are operating normally and the review of last month's backup generator failure at the station continues. "It's been a hard season for this community, and people kept showing up for work and for each other," Hale said. "That's a good thing to remember on Veterans Day."

At the depot: Corpus Christi Army Depot remains at full production with parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi.

For families: With the channel open, expect more ship and truck traffic around the port and along the waterfront in the coming days. If a family member asks you about the brigade's plans, please don't speculate online. Rumors travel faster than facts.

item.title: This week: depot back at full production, station power steady, brigade still waiting on the channel
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Our weekly roundup for families at NAS Corpus Christi, the Army depot and NAS Kingsville, one week after the blast at the jetties.
item.content:encoded:
It has been a long fall, and this week brought at least one piece of good news: Corpus Christi Army Depot is back at full production.

"Our workforce has been through a hurricane, a damaged hangar and weeks of standing by, and they came back every time," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a depot public affairs specialist. "Parts support from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi has been a big part of getting the lines moving again. We're grateful to our neighbors there and to the families who carried a lot while we got here."

At NAS Corpus Christi, power has been steady since the station's backup generator failed during a power interruption last month. Lt. Marcus Hale, a station public affairs officer, said the cause remains under review. "Power was restored, and base services are operating," Hale said. "We'll share what we can when the review is complete."

The channel: The Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed after the Oct. 28 explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties. The Navy has said the blast was caused by an explosive device. The Coast Guard is working with Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams to search the channel. We will not report on their work beyond what public affairs releases, and we ask readers to do the same on social media.

The brigade: A Fort Hood aviation brigade's move through the port for an overseas rotation has been delayed again by the closure. Fort Hood has not announced a new date. Families with loved ones in the brigade should rely on their unit's family readiness channels for updates.

Around the bases: Daylight saving time ends at 2 a.m. Sunday, so set your clocks back an hour. Several readers have asked about a fall community gathering; we will print details when organizers confirm them.

If the past two months have been heavy for your household, you are not alone. Chaplains and family support staff are available on both installations. Reach out early, and check on your neighbors.

item.title: Army depot back at full production, with parts support from DLA
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Corpus Christi Army Depot says work is back at full speed after Hurricane Rafael's hangar damage, with parts flowing from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi. After a hard week, some good news.
item.content:encoded:
After a week of hard headlines, here's one we've been waiting six weeks to write: Corpus Christi Army Depot is back at full production.

"This is our workforce's day," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a depot public affairs specialist. "They secured the aircraft before the storm, they waited through the damage, and they came back ready. We couldn't have gotten here without our partners at DLA Distribution Corpus Christi keeping the parts moving."

The depot halted work and secured helicopters in its hangars ahead of Hurricane Rafael. Rafael damaged hangar roofs and let water in, and employees were told to stand by. Now the shop floors are back at full speed, with parts support from the Defense Logistics Agency's distribution site at Corpus Christi.

For the depot's civilian workforce, many of them helicopter mechanics and technicians who live across the Coastal Bend, full production means full schedules again. The depot was hiring mechanics before the storm. "There's plenty to do, and these are the people who know how to do it," Kowalczyk said.

AROUND THE AREA THIS WEEK: The ship channel remains closed while Navy and Coast Guard teams search it after Thursday's explosion near the Port Aransas jetties, which the Navy says was caused by an explosive device. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement has been delayed again. Separately, the FBI said Sunday it traced the GPS interference pilots reported this month to a transmitter in a parked vehicle near an Inner Harbor fuel terminal. Get your updates from official sources.

HAPPY HALLOWEEN: If you're trick-or-treating tonight, carry a flashlight, check candy before the kids dig in, and slow down on neighborhood streets. And save us a peanut butter cup.

item.title: Special edition: Navy says an explosive device caused the jetty blast. What families should know
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Navy and Coast Guard teams are searching the ship channel and the FBI is investigating. The air station reports no impact to operations.
item.content:encoded:
The Navy said today that the explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties early Thursday was caused by an explosive device. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are searching the ship channel with the Coast Guard, and the FBI is investigating.

Two members of the tug's crew were injured in the blast. The Coast Guard has closed the channel.

"Navy teams are working with the Coast Guard to search the channel carefully and methodically," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "Safety comes first. We will not discuss the device or how the search is being conducted."

We know that leaves questions. Here is what we can tell families.

Are the bases affected? "There is no impact to operations at the air station," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. He said he would not discuss security measures. Follow the guards' instructions at the gates, carry your ID and build in extra time.

What about the Fort Hood unit waiting on the port? The aviation brigade's move through the port, already postponed by the hurricane, is delayed again while the channel is closed.

Stay off the water near the jetties. Boaters and anglers should stay clear of the entrance channel and obey any safety zone the Coast Guard sets. If you see something floating that does not look right, do not touch it. Move away and call the Coast Guard or 911.

Talk to your kids. Children hear more than we think. Tell them the truth in small pieces: something dangerous was found in the water, people whose job it is are dealing with it, and the grown-ups at home are safe.

Do not pass along rumors. You will see confident posts about who did this and why. Officials have not said. Sharing guesses does not help the people doing the work, and it can frighten the people you love.

If you know something. Anyone with information should contact the FBI.

Our thoughts are with the injured crew members and their families. We will update this story as the Navy and Coast Guard release more.

item.title: Special edition: Channel closure delays Fort Hood brigade's port movement again
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: The Army says a Fort Hood aviation brigade's move through the Port of Corpus Christi is delayed again by the ship channel closure. Here's what families on our bases should know.
item.content:encoded:
This is a special edition of Anchor & Rotor. Thursday's explosion near the Port Aransas jetties has consequences that reach beyond the waterfront, and we want our families to have the facts.

THE BLAST: Around 1 a.m. Thursday, an explosion went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties. It damaged the tug and hurt two crew members. The Coast Guard closed the ship channel. Officials say the cause is unknown.

THE BRIGADE: A Fort Hood aviation brigade has been scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi for an overseas rotation. That movement was postponed in September as Hurricane Rafael approached. The Army said Friday it has been delayed again by the channel closure.

"The brigade remains ready to deploy when the port is ready," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. "This closure delays our port movement again. Our soldiers and families have been flexible through a lot, and we'll move when it's safe to move."

WHAT IT MEANS HERE: The brigade is based at Fort Hood, not in the Coastal Bend, but many of our readers have friends, relatives and former shipmates in Army aviation, and the port is part of our community. If you have a loved one in the brigade, their unit's family readiness group is the best place for updates. Please don't share details about unit movements online, even well-meaning ones.

TAKING CARE: The past six weeks have been a lot: the storm, the water notice, a generator failure at the station, and now this. If your kids are asking about the explosion, keep answers simple and honest. Something happened on the water, people are investigating, and grown-ups are working to keep everyone safe.

We'll publish updates as officials release them.

item.title: Station backup generator failed during power interruption; power restored
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: NAS Corpus Christi says a backup generator failed during a power interruption over the weekend. Power is back, and the cause is under review.
item.content:encoded:
Naval Air Station Corpus Christi's backup generator failed during a power interruption over the weekend, the station said Monday. Power has been restored, and the cause of the generator failure is under review.

"Power is restored, and we're reviewing what happened with the backup generator," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station. "We appreciate everyone's patience. Families with questions about services should check the station's official channels for the latest information."

The station did not say how long the interruption lasted or which facilities were affected, and Hale declined to discuss details while the review is under way.

If your household or workplace on the station lost power, a few practical reminders. When in doubt about refrigerated food, throw it out. Check medications that need refrigeration and call your pharmacy if you're unsure. Reset alarms and medical devices that may have restarted. And if you rely on powered medical equipment, make sure your family's emergency plan includes a backup, whether that's a battery pack or a neighbor's outlet.

It has been a long six weeks for the station. Aircraft flew to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth ahead of Hurricane Rafael and came home after the storm. The Army depot that shares the station has been working through hangar roof damage and water intrusion. And this month the station has hosted a ten-day relief airlift of 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charters for the Coastal Bend.

Through it all, the station's families have done what military families do: adjusted, pitched in and kept the kids fed. The generator review is one more thing to watch, and Anchor & Rotor will share the results when the station releases them.

item.title: FAA notice on GPS interference: relief flights continue, and most of the city can drink the tap water again
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Crews flying aid into the air station are using backup navigation, the station says. The citywide boil-water notice has been lifted; Districts 3 and 4 must keep boiling.
item.content:encoded:
Two pieces of news for station families this Saturday, one from the sky and one from the kitchen sink.

GPS interference notice. Pilots have reported interference with GPS signals within about 40 miles of Corpus Christi, and the Federal Aviation Administration has issued a notice to aviators. Relief flights into Naval Air Station Corpus Christi are continuing using backup navigation.

"Our crews train for this," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the air station. "Flights are continuing safely with backup navigation procedures, and there is no impact to the relief mission or to station operations."

Hale said he could not discuss the cause of the interference. The FAA has not given one.

What it means for families. Not much on the ground. You will keep seeing and hearing the big gray jets. The airlift that began Monday is bringing in relief supplies on 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charters over ten days. If you fly or boat for fun, check official notices before you go.

Please do not speculate online about what is behind the interference. Rumors travel faster than facts, and we have all had enough of those this fall.

The boil-water notice is over for most of us. The city lifted the citywide boil-water notice today after pump repairs at the water treatment plant and a round of testing. It lasted five weeks. Before you drink from the tap, run cold water for a few minutes to flush your pipes, dump the ice in your ice maker and make a few fresh batches, change refrigerator and pitcher filters, and run the dishwasher empty once.

One exception. A separate boil-water notice remains in effect for Water Districts 3 and 4. If you live there, keep boiling until the city lifts that notice.

A thank-you. To every family that hauled jugs, shared a camp stove or drove a neighbor to a water distribution site: this community noticed.

Our regular edition returns next week.

item.title: This week on base: relief jets, depot repairs and a month of getting back to normal
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: The relief airlift is halfway through its ten-day run, and the Army depot's workforce is working through storm damage. Here's the roundup.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to this week's roundup. If you live on or near Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, you've already heard the biggest news of the week. It has been flying over your roof.

AIRLIFT: Relief flights began landing Monday, part of a ten-day airlift of 26 military C-17s and 14 civilian charters. "Thank you to our families and neighbors for their patience with the extra activity," said Lt. Marcus Hale, NAS Corpus Christi public affairs. "Every one of those aircraft is carrying help for the Coastal Bend."

DEPOT: At Corpus Christi Army Depot, crews are still working through the hangar roof damage and water intrusion the storm left behind. "Our workforce has been patient and resilient through all of this," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a depot public affairs specialist. "These are people who take real pride in their work, and they want to be back on the floor doing it. We're getting there, step by step."

TRAINING: The training aircraft that rode out the storm at NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth began coming home six days after landfall. If you have a student aviator at home, you know the airplanes came back weeks ago; the rest of life is still catching up.

OFF BASE: Replacement pump parts arrived at the city's O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant on Wednesday, but the city's boil-water notice remains in effect until installation and testing are done. If you live off base in Corpus Christi, keep boiling tap water until the city says otherwise.

STAY SHARP ONLINE: False rumors and phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal have circulated since the storm. Get base news from official station channels, and don't click links in unsolicited messages, no matter how official they look.

That's the week. Hug your people, and thank a flight-line worker if you know one.

item.title: Relief airlift begins at NAS Corpus Christi: what families should know
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Forty relief flights, military C-17s and civilian charters, are due at the air station over the next ten days. Expect bigger aircraft and more noise.
item.content:encoded:
If the windows rattle a little more than usual this week, here's why: relief flights have started landing at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi.

Over the next ten days, 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charter flights are scheduled to bring relief supplies into the station, according to NAS Corpus Christi public affairs. For a base whose skies usually belong to training aircraft, that is a lot of very large airplanes.

"The air station is proud to support the relief effort for our neighbors across the Coastal Bend," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for NAS Corpus Christi. "Families may notice larger aircraft and more activity around the airfield. We'll put out notices through official channels if anything changes for base services."

The airlift caps a long month for the station. Training aircraft flew to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth ahead of Hurricane Rafael and began returning six days after landfall. Corpus Christi Army Depot, which sits on the station, reported hangar roof damage and water intrusion from the storm and told workers to stand by.

The flights also begin a day after the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider unloaded 40 relief containers at the Port of Corpus Christi, about a month late, after waiting in the anchorage backlog. Help is now arriving by sea and by air.

A few reminders for families this week. Expect daytime aircraft noise, and plan naps and nervous pets accordingly. Get base news from official station channels, not from screenshots. And if you see a post that seems designed to make you angry or afraid, check it before you share it; false rumors and lookalike aid sites have circulated widely since the storm.

Thank you, as always, for being good neighbors. Anchor & Rotor will keep track of the airlift through the week.

item.title: Port of Corpus Christi and CBPWA announce joint counter-UAS program after unauthorized drone activity identified pre-storm
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: The Port of Corpus Christi Authority and Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority announced a joint counter-drone detection program Saturday, acting on the federal finding, made public two weeks ago, of unauthorized drone activity in the area before Hurricane Rafael's landfall.
item.content:encoded:
The Port of Corpus Christi Authority and Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority jointly announced Saturday the deployment of a counter-uncrewed aerial systems monitoring program covering critical infrastructure at the port and utility facilities, following the federal finding, made public Sept. 29, of unauthorized drone activity in the area before the storm. It is the first step either agency has announced in response.

"Port of Corpus Christi Authority and CBPWA today announced a joint counter-UAS monitoring program for critical infrastructure, following retroactive identification of unauthorized drone activity in the pre-storm period," the joint statement reads. The agencies did not specify the dates on which the drone activity was identified, the type or number of aircraft involved, or the specific facilities overflown. They said the program will deploy a radio-frequency detection and direction-finding network at sites across the port and utility corridor, supplied by Sentinel Airspace Inc. and expected to be operational within 90 days.

Counter-UAS authority for civilian infrastructure is tightly restricted under federal law, which currently limits most countermeasures to federal law enforcement and the Department of Defense. The joint program is limited to detection: it can locate a drone and its operator but cannot bring an aircraft down. The agencies said the network will be operated in coordination with the FAA and CBP Air and Marine Operations.

The disclosure that drone activity was retroactively identified above critical infrastructure in the pre-storm period is significant in the context of the confirmed cyberattack on CBPWA's industrial control systems and the broader federal investigation. Law enforcement officials have not publicly discussed the drone activity or its potential relationship to the cyberattack; the FBI declined to comment Saturday. Aviation security specialists noted that pre-attack drone reconnaissance of industrial facilities has been documented in other infrastructure incident investigations.

Port spokesperson Javier Salinas and CBPWA did not answer specific questions about the drone findings at Saturday's briefing. "Our focus is on protecting the facilities going forward," Salinas said. "We identified a gap. We are closing it." The FAA's temporary flight restriction over the area in September was the hurricane restriction and is unrelated to the new program.

item.title: Four weeks after Rafael: where things stand for base families
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Aircraft are back, the depot is still repairing hangars, the boil-water notice continues and household aid from FEMA has been requested but not approved.
item.content:encoded:
Tuesday marks four weeks since Hurricane Rafael came ashore. For many station and depot families, life is a mix of normal routines and stubborn leftovers: a tarp on the roof, a pot of water on the stove. Here is where things stand.

Aircraft and flying. Training aircraft that were flown to Fort Worth before the storm have returned to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi and Naval Air Station Kingsville. "Our squadrons are back and training," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the air station.

The depot. Corpus Christi Army Depot is still repairing hangar roof damage and water intrusion from the storm. "Our people want to get back to full speed, and we are getting there building by building," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot. Employees with questions about their status should check with their supervisors.

Water. The citywide boil-water notice is still in effect. Bring water to a rolling boil for two minutes before you drink it, cook with it or brush your teeth. The city says replacement parts for the damaged pumps at the water plant were delayed because the supplier's local warehouse flooded; the parts are shipping from out of state.

Night skies. No new sightings of lights or drones over the air station have been reported in recent weeks. The FBI has confirmed it is looking into the earlier reports. "We are aware of the reports and continue to work with the appropriate authorities," Hale said. "There has been no impact to operations." If you see something, report it to base security rather than posting it.

Federal help for households. The state has formally asked FEMA to add Individual Assistance, the program that helps households directly. It has not been approved yet. When it is, we will walk you through registration. Until then, keep your receipts and photos, and remember that no one can charge you a fee to apply for FEMA aid.

Scams. Watch for emails that imitate a disaster-aid website. Type web addresses yourself and do not click links in messages you did not expect.

Need help now? Your installation's family support office and the relief societies can assist with emergency needs. Ask. That is what they are there for.

item.title: Week in review: emergency fuel contract appears in federal records; boil-water notice stretches on
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Records show a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for NAS Corpus Christi after the station's regular supplier flooded. Off-base families keep boiling as pump parts are delayed, and the bay fishing closure is extended.
item.content:encoded:
Here's what families need to know this week.

Fuel contract. Federal contract records show a $2.1 million emergency fuel contract for NAS Corpus Christi went to Quellmar Fuel Partners, a Corpus Christi fuel company, after the station's regular supplier flooded in Hurricane Rafael. The Bayside Ledger first reported the records Monday. "We're glad to help keep the station supplied while its regular supplier recovers," Quellmar operations manager Nadia Kerr told Anchor & Rotor. We'll pass along any station guidance for families as it's issued.

Water. Off-base households in Corpus Christi remain under the city's boil-water notice. The city says replacement parts for the damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens plant are delayed because the supplier's local warehouse flooded, and the parts are shipping from out of state. No date has been set to lift the notice. Keep boiling water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, ice and formula.

Fishing. If your family fishes the bays on weekends, hold off. Texas Parks and Wildlife on Tuesday extended its fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and shellfish harvesting there remains closed by the state health department. Don't eat anything caught there, and keep kids and pets away from any oil on the shoreline.

Quiet skies. There have been no new drone reports since late September. The FBI's investigation into the earlier reports continues. As always, please don't post speculation about base security online.

Back home. Training aircraft have been returning from NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth since Sept. 20. If you live near the field, you've heard them. Some of you have written to say it's the best noise in town.

Self-care. Three weeks of boiling, hauling and cleaning take a toll on everyone. Military OneSource and your installation's family support programs offer free, confidential counseling. Take the help.

Have news from your unit, your street or your family readiness group? Send it in. We'll keep this space for you.

item.title: Families: Quieter nights, an easing stomach bug and a fake aid site to avoid
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: No new drone sightings have been reported near NAS Corpus Christi, stomach illness is easing, and a researcher warns about a lookalike aid website. Here's this week's roundup.
item.content:encoded:
Two and a half weeks after Rafael, many of you have told us the same thing: the days are getting more routine, even if the routine includes boiling water. Here's what's new this week.

Quiet skies. No new drone sightings have been reported near NAS Corpus Christi after about ten days of reports following the storm. The FBI has confirmed it is investigating the earlier reports. "We continue to work with the appropriate authorities, and there's no impact to operations," said Lt. Marcus Hale, NAS Corpus Christi public affairs officer. As always, we won't report on security measures, and we ask readers not to post speculation about the base online.

Stomach bug easing. The health district says emergency room visits for stomach illness have begun to ease after last week's surge. Keep up the hand-washing with soap and boiled or bottled water, and keep sick kids home for two days after symptoms stop. Child care providers will thank you.

Still boiling. Off-base households in Corpus Christi remain under the city's boil-water notice. Temporary pumps are limiting capacity while the plant waits on replacement parts for its damaged pumps, the city says. No date has been given for lifting the notice.

Watch that link. A threat researcher says rumor posts after the storm were coordinated across about 40 accounts and pointed people to a lookalike aid site, aid-help-portal.example, which also appeared in phishing emails. Do not enter personal or banking information on it. If you get an email asking you to "verify" aid information, delete it. Service members should also report suspicious emails through their command's procedures.

Depot update. Corpus Christi Army Depot employees should continue to follow guidance from their supervisors on returning to work.

Friday night. A reader from Flour Bluff sent us a photo of her kids' youth football practice this week: a cooler of bottled water on the sideline and a parent stationed at the hand-washing jug. Small things. They matter.

Thanks to everyone who sent in notes. Keep them coming.

item.title: Federal Agencies Open Probe into Pre-Storm Drone Flights Near Corpus Christi Utilities
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: A joint FAA and CBP statement confirms that multiple incidents of unauthorized unmanned aircraft operations in the Corpus Christi area in the days before Hurricane Rafael are now under federal investigation.
item.content:encoded:
Federal aviation and border security authorities issued a joint statement Wednesday confirming that investigators have identified multiple incidents of unauthorized unmanned aircraft system operations in the Corpus Christi area in the period leading up to Hurricane Rafael. The agencies did not say how many flights were involved, where they took place or when; they asked anyone with information about drone activity in the area between September 4 and September 12 to contact the FBI.

The statement from the Federal Aviation Administration and U.S. Customs and Border Protection Air and Marine Operations says the aircraft operated without required FAA authorizations and were detected through a combination of radar and electronic sensor records. "Due to the ongoing nature of the investigation, no additional details about the number, location, or timing of the incidents can be released at this time," the statement reads. Neither agency attributed the drone flights to any actor, country, or intent.

CBP Air and Marine Operations operates counter-UAS detection infrastructure along the Texas Gulf Coast as part of its border security mission, and that infrastructure captured the tracks in question during routine pre-storm operations. The FAA's Office of Security and Hazardous Materials Safety is participating in the review alongside CBP and unspecified federal law enforcement partners. The flights passed over or near infrastructure corridors that include water pumping stations, electrical transmission facilities, and pipeline infrastructure, according to federal sources who spoke on condition of anonymity because the investigation is ongoing. The flight patterns, Anchor and Rotor Weekly has confirmed through aviation sources, are consistent with slow, loitering behavior over fixed points of interest.

Aviation security experts caution against premature conclusions. "Pre-storm drone activity near infrastructure is not automatically evidence of hostile intent," said retired Air Force Lt. Col. Dena Carver, who now consults on UAS security. "It could be media, insurance assessment, environmental monitoring. The investigation will determine what it was." Federal authorities have not publicly linked the drone flights to any other aspect of the post-storm situation in Corpus Christi. No suspects have been identified and no charges have been filed. The FAA and CBP say they will not provide further public comment while the investigation is active.

item.title: Week in review: aircraft back on the ramp, FBI looking into drone reports
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Training aircraft are returning to the Coastal Bend's air stations, the FBI confirms it is investigating drone reports near NAS Corpus Christi, and the depot keeps its workforce on standby.
item.content:encoded:
It has been a long ten days, and this week brought some welcome normal. Here's what families need to know.

Aircraft are home. Training aircraft that evacuated to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth before Hurricane Rafael began returning to NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville on Monday. As always, we don't report aircraft numbers or schedules. "Every day we get a little closer to normal," said Lt. Marcus Hale, NAS Corpus Christi public affairs officer.

Drone reports. The FBI's Houston division confirmed this week that it is investigating reports of drones near the air station. "We can confirm we are investigating," spokesperson Mark Ellery said Thursday. "We have no further comment." Earlier in the week the station said it is aware of the reports and working with authorities, with no impact to operations. Hale asked families to report anything unusual to police and to avoid passing along rumors. "If you see something, report it. Please don't speculate online," he said.

Depot. Corpus Christi Army Depot's workforce remains on standby while hangars damaged by the storm are assessed. "Take care of your homes and your families," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a depot public affairs specialist. "We'll call you back as soon as the buildings are safe, and you'll hear it from your supervisor first."

Health. Emergency rooms in Nueces County are seeing about 180% more stomach-illness visits than normal, and wastewater testing shows norovirus is circulating. Keep sick kids home, wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water, and watch little ones closely for signs of dehydration.

Water. Off-base households in Corpus Christi remain under the city's boil-water notice. The city said Friday that the water plant's damaged pumps need replacement parts and that temporary pumps are limiting capacity. No date has been given for lifting the notice.

Thank you. To the spouses running carpools and water runs, the neighbors with generators keeping phones charged, and everyone checking on new families who don't know anyone here yet: thank you. It shows.

item.title: Coast Guard files formal SAR incident report: 1,427 rescues, 341 by helicopter, operation complete
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi has filed Incident Summary Report ISR-2027-CC-004 formally closing the Hurricane Rafael search-and-rescue operation with 1,427 confirmed rescues, 341 of them by helicopter.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — The U.S. Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi filed Incident Summary Report ISR-2027-CC-004 on Tuesday, formally archiving the Hurricane Rafael search-and-rescue operation and certifying its final statistics: 1,427 confirmed rescues — 341 by helicopter hoist, 1,041 by surface vessel and 45 ambulatory survivor contacts — over an operational period from the first launch at 1:22 a.m. on September 14 through stand-down on September 19.

The ISR, a formal Coast Guard record required for all major SAR incidents, was submitted to Coast Guard District 8 and will serve as the authoritative source document for the operational record of the rescue phase of the Rafael response. Sector Corpus Christi Commander Capt. Delia Ostrowski-Han signed the report as the cognizant Coast Guard authority. "This document is not a celebration," Ostrowski-Han said at a Tuesday morning briefing. "It is a record of an extraordinary effort under the worst conditions this community has faced in decades. The numbers represent real people whose lives were saved by the men and women of the Coast Guard, the fire department, the sheriff's office, and Task Force 1."

The ISR documents the operational sequencing of the rescue effort, from the initial activation of Air Station Corpus Christi's alert crews before Rafael's landfall through the final grid sweeps of south Mustang Island on the fifth day of operations. It notes the critical role of thermal imaging from the HH-60 Jayhawks in locating survivors during the nighttime hours immediately following landfall, when ground-based rescue units were unable to safely enter the surge zone. The document also acknowledges the unprecedented call volume handled by the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center — about 2,900 calls in a single day — as a key factor in the coordination of multi-agency rescue assets.

The report will be submitted to the Coast Guard's Rescue 21 SAR database and to the Interagency Committee on Search and Rescue for statistical archiving. Anchor and Rotor Weekly has obtained a summary of the ISR through a Coast Guard public affairs request. The 23 confirmed fatalities remain under investigation by the Nueces County Medical Examiner, with final cause-of-death determinations expected within 60 to 90 days. The Coast Guard will conduct a formal lessons-learned debrief with its SAR partners in the coming months.

item.title: Training aircraft begin returning to NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Aircraft that rode out Rafael at NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth are coming home. Station officials also say they are aware of residents' reports of drones and are working with authorities.
item.content:encoded:
Training aircraft that flew north ahead of Hurricane Rafael began returning to NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville on Monday, station officials said, a sight many families had been waiting for since the planes left for NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth before the storm.

"Seeing our aircraft back on the ramp is a big step for the whole team," said Lt. Marcus Hale, NAS Corpus Christi public affairs officer. "Our people have worked hard to get the airfield ready, and we're grateful to our hosts in Fort Worth for keeping the aircraft safe."

As always, Anchor & Rotor does not report aircraft numbers or flight schedules. Squadron members should follow their chain of command for duty and reporting guidance.

Hale also addressed the videos many of you have seen on social media since last week showing lights hovering over the air station at night. "NAS Corpus Christi is aware of the reports of drones and is working with the appropriate authorities," he said. "There is no impact to operations." He declined to discuss security measures, which the station does not comment on.

At Corpus Christi Army Depot, crews are still dealing with the hangar roof damage and water intrusion the depot reported Friday. Depot employees were told to stand by and should watch for word from their supervisors on returning to work.

For families: Off-base households in Corpus Christi remain under the city's boil-water notice issued Saturday. Boil tap water at a rolling boil for two minutes before drinking, cooking, brushing teeth or mixing formula, or use bottled water.

Health officials also reported Monday that wastewater testing shows norovirus and that stomach illness visits are rising. Wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water, keep sick children home, and check in on neighbors who may not have water or transportation.

If you need help, your command's family readiness contacts are the first stop. We'll keep updating as the station shares more.

item.title: 1,427 survivors: Combined SAR operation stands down after five days; transition to recovery begins
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: The joint search-and-rescue operation launched after Hurricane Rafael officially stood down Sunday evening with 1,427 confirmed rescues across all agencies, as commanders declare all accessible areas swept and shift to recovery operations.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — The combined search-and-rescue operation for Hurricane Rafael was formally stood down Sunday evening after five days of continuous operations, with the joint command announcing a confirmed total of 1,427 rescues across all participating agencies — a number that Corpus Christi Fire Chief Alberto Rincón called "an extraordinary testament to the dedication of every person who put a boat in the water or a helicopter in the air in this operation."

Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center Dispatch Chief Elena Vasquez-Okafor and Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi Commander Capt. Delia Ostrowski-Han made the announcement jointly at a late-afternoon press briefing, declaring that all areas accessible by water, ground vehicle, and air asset had been systematically swept and that the operation was transitioning from active search-and-rescue to recovery mode. Under that transition, the focus shifts from locating living survivors to searching for and recovering the remains of those who did not survive, a task that will be managed by law enforcement and medical examiner personnel rather than rescue units.

"We went into every flooded street and every damaged neighborhood that our teams could physically reach," Ostrowski-Han said. "Some streets could not be reached by boat or on foot for the first 48 hours because of surge depth and debris, and there the helicopter crews did the work. Those areas have since been cleared. We are confident that the rescue phase has ended." She noted that the pace had slowed since Thursday evening, when the count stood at 702, and that the last rescues were logged Sunday afternoon.

The 1,427 rescue figure represents a combined count across CCFD swift-water teams, U.S. Coast Guard helicopter and boat crews from Air Station Corpus Christi and Sector Corpus Christi, Nueces County Sheriff's Office marine deputies, Texas Task Force 1 rescue specialists, and multiple mutual aid fire and rescue departments from the surrounding region. Coast Guard and partner helicopter crews accounted for 341 of the rescues, most of them by hoist from rooftops and debris fields, with the remaining evacuations conducted by boat and on foot. The 23 fatalities confirmed as of the stand-down are under investigation by the Nueces County Medical Examiner's office.

item.title: Week one after Rafael: Boil your water, watch for scam emails, and depot workers keep standing by
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Our weekly roundup for families at NAS Corpus Christi, Corpus Christi Army Depot and NAS Kingsville: what changed this week and what to watch for.
item.content:encoded:
It's been a long week. Thank you for checking in, and thank you to every neighbor who checked on someone else. Here's where things stand as of Sunday afternoon.

Boil your water. The city issued a citywide boil-water notice Saturday. Bring tap water to a rolling boil for two minutes before drinking, cooking, brushing teeth or mixing formula, or use bottled water. City water distribution sites are open.

Watch your inbox. The City of Corpus Christi has warned its employees and residents about phishing emails dressed up as a disaster-aid portal. Don't click links in unexpected aid emails, and never enter a password or bank information through one. Go to official sites directly. The same caution applies to your work email: If something looks off, report it through your command's normal channels.

Depot workers: Keep standing by. Corpus Christi Army Depot reported hangar roof damage and water intrusion, and workers have been told to stand by until they hear from their supervisors, depot spokesperson Brenda Kowalczyk said Friday.

Bridges are open. The Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway reopened Friday after inspections, so commuters from Portland and Ingleside can cross the bay again.

Stay off oiled shorelines. Oil from the Inner Harbor spill reached North Beach, the Portland shoreline and Nueces Bay marshes. Texas Parks and Wildlife has closed fishing and the Texas Department of State Health Services has closed shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, and health officials say to avoid contact with the oil.
