That includes the fishing spots many of you love along the bay.

About those posts. Station officials said this week that claims the military is seizing homes are false. Some readers have also asked about videos posted online showing lights over the station at night. The station has not commented publicly on them; we will share any statement when there is one.

Aircraft. The training aircraft remain at Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth for now. We'll report return plans as soon as they're announced.

item.title: Army depot reports hangar roof damage and water intrusion; workers told to stand by
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Corpus Christi Army Depot employees should wait for word from supervisors before reporting. Station officials also say posts claiming the military is seizing homes are false.
item.content:encoded:
Corpus Christi Army Depot reported hangar roof damage and water intrusion from Hurricane Rafael, and workers are being told to stand by until further notice, a depot spokesperson said Friday.

"Our workforce is the heart of this depot, and right now we want every one of them focused on their families and their homes," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot. "We'll bring people back as soon as it's safe to do the work. Until then, please stand by for word from your supervisor."

The depot, the military's primary center for helicopter repair and overhaul, halted work and secured helicopters in its hangars before the storm. Kowalczyk did not detail the extent of the damage. In keeping with our practice, Anchor & Rotor does not report specifics about facilities or aircraft beyond what public affairs releases.

For the depot's civilian workforce, many of whom live across the Coastal Bend, the wait comes on top of storm damage at home and low water pressure across the city. One piece of good news arrived Friday morning: The Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway reopened after inspections, so employees who live in Portland and Ingleside can cross the bay again when the call comes.

Some families have asked us about posts claiming the military is seizing homes damaged in the storm. Station officials say that is false. "That rumor is false, full stop," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer at NAS Corpus Christi. "No one's home is being taken."

The training aircraft from NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville remain at Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth. We'll report return plans when they are announced.

Employees with questions should contact their supervisors. Spouses and families can reach out through their family readiness groups. We'll keep this page updated through the weekend.

item.title: Storm special: What base families need to know after Rafael
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Water pressure is low across the city, both bridges over the bay are closed and the training aircraft are still in Fort Worth. Here is a guide for the days ahead.
item.content:encoded:
To every family reading this by flashlight or on a phone you're trying to keep charged: We are thinking of you. Rafael struck Mustang Island in the early hours of Tuesday, around 1 a.m., as a Category 3 storm, and the days ahead will be hard ones for everyone in the Coastal Bend, on base and off.

Water. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both of its power feeds early in the storm, and pumps were damaged. Water pressure is low across Corpus Christi, including in the Flour Bluff neighborhoods where many of our families live. The city is asking everyone to conserve. Save what you have for drinking, cooking and basic hygiene.

Roads. The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway are closed until inspections are complete. If you live in Portland, Ingleside or elsewhere across the bay, the direct routes into Corpus Christi are shut. Talk to your supervisor before you try to commute, and never drive into floodwater to get to work.

Aircraft and the depot. The training aircraft flown from NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth before the storm remain there. Corpus Christi Army Depot halted work and secured its helicopters in hangars before Rafael arrived. We will share return plans and depot updates as soon as public affairs releases them.

Information. Rely on your command, your family readiness group and official installation channels. Be careful with anything shared online that you can't trace back to an official source; storms bring rumors.

Check in. If you evacuated, make sure your command knows where you are. If you stayed, check on your neighbors, especially spouses whose service member is away.

Most of all, take care of each other. We'll be back with more as the picture comes into focus.

item.title: Coast Guard Jayhawks fly 180 hoists over Flour Bluff and North Beach as thermal imaging cuts through debris field
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: HH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crews from Air Station Corpus Christi have completed 180 hoist operations since launching early Tuesday, with thermal imaging cameras credited for locating survivors hidden beneath debris in flooded neighborhoods.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — Helicopter crews from U.S. Coast Guard Air Station Corpus Christi have completed 180 hoist operations in Flour Bluff, North Beach and surrounding low-lying neighborhoods since launching at 1:22 a.m. Tuesday, working in improving but still challenging conditions following Hurricane Rafael's passage. Thermal imaging sensors carried by the station's HH-60 Jayhawk aircraft have been credited with locating multiple survivors who were not visible from above due to debris cover or who were sheltering beneath partially collapsed roof structures.

Air Station Corpus Christi Commander Capt. Darlene Osei said her crews launched as soon as the eyewall had passed and winds dropped to within operational limits, flying in winds of up to 55 knots. "We were wheels-up minutes after the worst of it and we have been flying continuously since," Osei said at a brief afternoon press availability outside the operations building at NAS-CC. "Every rescue is a family that made a decision to stay or couldn't leave, and we are out there bringing them home."

The FLIR thermal imaging system carried on the Jayhawks allowed rescue swimmers and flight mechanics to identify body heat signatures through roof debris and vegetation, a capability that proved critical in Flour Bluff, where surge flooding of four to six feet deposited substantial debris across residential neighborhoods. In several rescues, the IR camera detected survivors beneath a collapsed carport or inside a structure where the outer walls had partially separated from the roof. Rescue swimmers were lowered by hoist to reach those individuals once the aircraft commander confirmed a safe working zone.

The Coast Guard said 341 people had been rescued by air as of 3 p.m. Wednesday, with boat and ground crews adding 145 more for a total of 486. The cumulative count is continuing to climb as additional ground assets — Corpus Christi Fire Department swift-water teams, Nueces County Sheriff's Office boat units, and Texas Task Force 1 — begin working flooded neighborhoods that the helicopter units have identified but not yet reached. The rescue count was expected to increase significantly through Wednesday evening as the full extent of storm surge flooding in south Mustang Island and the Flour Bluff area becomes clearer. NAS Corpus Christi also made its flight line available for staging of additional Coast Guard and National Guard rotary assets arriving from other sectors in support of the SAR operation.

item.title: Special edition: Rafael is hours away. A last checklist for base families
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: A Category 3 landfall is expected near Port Aransas early Tuesday. If you are in Zones A, B or C, leave now. Here is what the bases are saying and what to take.
item.content:encoded:
Hurricane Rafael strengthened to a Category 3 today and is expected to make landfall near Port Aransas between midnight and 2 a.m. Tuesday, with 9 to 12 feet of storm surge. The Coastal Bend is under a hurricane warning. This is our last update before the storm.

If you are in an evacuation zone, go. Nueces County's mandatory evacuation order covers Zones A, B and C: all coastal areas, all areas below 10 feet of elevation and all mobile and manufactured homes countywide. Shelters are open inland. If you have not left and you are in one of those zones, leave now while you still can. If you need a ride, call 2-1-1.

The bases. Training aircraft from Naval Air Station Corpus Christi and Naval Air Station Kingsville were flown to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth last week. Corpus Christi Army Depot has halted work and secured helicopters in its hangars.

"Our aircraft are safe, and our focus now is on our people," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the air station. "Follow the evacuation order. Follow your chain of command's instructions. Check in when you get where you are going."

"The hangars are buttoned up and the workforce has been sent home to take care of their families," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot. "Nobody should come in until they are told it is safe."

If your service member went with the aircraft. Many spouses are doing this one alone. You are not the only one. Text your family readiness contact where you are headed and when you arrive. Take the folder: IDs, orders, insurance papers, medical records, the kids' shot records. Take medicines, chargers and the pets.

If you are staying outside the evacuation zones. Fill bathtubs and clean containers with water. Charge everything. Know which interior room you will use. Stay off the roads once the wind rises, and do not go outside during the calm of the eye.

After the storm. Do not come back until officials say roads are open. Do not drive through water. Expect power and phones to be out.

We will publish again as soon as we are able. Take care of each other.

item.title: FAA shuts Corpus Christi airspace: TFR-2027-CC-0441 suspends all commercial and general aviation ahead of Rafael
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: The FAA has issued a temporary flight restriction covering airspace within 30 nautical miles of Corpus Christi International to 18,000 feet, effective early Sunday morning, with NAS Corpus Christi exempted for emergency operations.
item.content:encoded:
The Federal Aviation Administration issued Temporary Flight Restriction TFR-2027-CC-0441 Sunday morning, ordering a complete suspension of commercial and general aviation operations over the Corpus Christi area effective at 00:01 local time Sunday, September 12, as Hurricane Rafael approaches the Texas coast.

The TFR covers airspace within 30 nautical miles of Corpus Christi International Airport from the surface to 18,000 feet mean sea level, encompassing a broad zone across the Coastal Bend sufficient to protect aerial operations during Rafael's passage and the immediate aftermath. FAA Southwest Region spokesperson Dale Hoffmeister confirmed that all regularly scheduled commercial service into and out of Corpus Christi International is suspended until the restriction is lifted, with no specific end time given pending storm passage and airspace assessment.

Naval Air Station Corpus Christi is specifically exempted from the TFR for emergency operations. Coast Guard Air Station Corpus Christi, which is collocated on the NAS-CC flight line, also retains authority to operate under the emergency operations carve-out. Military and Coast Guard aircraft supporting hurricane relief, search and rescue, or medical evacuation are authorized to fly within the restricted zone under coordination with the controlling agency.

"This is a standard protective measure for major hurricane events," Hoffmeister told Anchor and Rotor Weekly in a phone interview Sunday. "The TFR ensures that emergency aviation assets have clean airspace to operate in when conditions allow, without risk of conflict with general aviation or commercial traffic that has no business being in a storm zone."

Charter and general aviation operators based at Corpus Christi International and at Aransas County Airport in Rockport were advised to depart to airports outside the TFR boundary as soon as they could do so safely. Coast Guard Air Station Corpus Christi is currently staging additional HH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crews and C-144 aircraft for post-storm search and rescue operations within the now-protected airspace.

item.title: Special edition: Aircraft head to Fort Worth. A families' guide to the days ahead
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: With training aircraft moving out and the depot securing helicopters, here is what families should know and do now. Follow your command and county officials for any evacuation guidance.
item.content:encoded:
If you heard aircraft lifting off early this morning and wondered why, here is the answer. Training aircraft from NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville are headed to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth to get out of Hurricane Rafael's way. Corpus Christi Army Depot has halted work and secured its helicopters in hangars.

No hurricane watch has been issued yet, but the forecast cone covers Corpus Christi. That is why this special edition is coming out before our regular weekly issue.

"Families should follow their command's guidance and any county evacuation orders," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer at NAS Corpus Christi. "The most important thing you can do today is make sure your command can reach you. Navy families, check your information in NFAAS."

For depot employees and their families, the message is similar. "Take care of your families first," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist at the depot. "Keep your phone on, and watch for word from your supervisor about when to come back."

Your checklist for today:

Account for yourself. Update NFAAS if you are a Navy family. Army families and depot civilians, confirm your contact information with your unit or supervisor.

Grab the folder. IDs, orders, powers of attorney, insurance and medical records in one waterproof bag, with photos on your phone.

Fill up and cash out. Gas, prescriptions and cash, today.

Know your zone. If you live off base in a county evacuation zone, county orders apply to you like everyone else. Plan your destination now.

Need a ride? Call 2-1-1 to register for evacuation help.

Pets, kids, chargers. Everyone gets a bag. Every bag gets a charger.

A note on the aircraft move: if your service member is part of it, expect limited contact for a while, and please do not post details about schedules or locations. Public affairs will share what can be shared, and we will publish it here.

We will update this guide as installation public affairs offices release new information.

item.title: Rafael is a hurricane now. Here is what military families should do this week
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Use the quiet days to get ready, watch your command's official channels for guidance, and keep unit details off social media.
item.content:encoded:
Hurricane Rafael is in the Gulf, and forecasters warn it could strengthen rapidly over warm water. We do not know yet where it will go. We do know that the families who handle storms best are the ones who were ready before anyone asked them to be.

If you followed our family plan columns over the last few weeks, this is the week you use them. If you did not, start here.

Finish the folder. IDs, orders, powers of attorney, insurance, medical records and a list of medications, all in one waterproof folder, with photos on your phone.

Fill up. Gas tanks, prescriptions and cash. Card readers and pumps do not work without power.

Update your contact information. Navy families, check NFAAS today. Army families and depot civilians, confirm how your unit or supervisor will reach you.

Make the one-adult plan. Service members and many depot employees may have duties before and after a storm. Plan as if the adult at home will do the evacuation alone.

Need a ride? County emergency managers urge residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance by calling 2-1-1. That includes families who share one car with a service member.

Watch official channels. Guidance for families will come from your command and from installation public affairs offices. We will publish it here as soon as it is released.

Keep it off social media. If you hear about aircraft schedules, unit plans or who is going where, please do not post it. Let public affairs release what can be released. That protects your service member and your neighbors.

Talk with your kids. Give them one job each. Kids handle a plan better than a surprise.

Base services continue to operate normally as of this morning. Check your command's channels before you head to any facility in the days ahead.

item.title: Tropical Storm Rafael forms far to the south: no threat yet, but check your kit this Labor Day weekend
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: The new storm is a long way from Texas and there are no watches for our coast. Forecasters say it is a good weekend to get ready anyway.
item.content:encoded:
A tropical storm named Rafael formed Saturday in the northwestern Caribbean Sea. It is a long way from Texas, and there are no watches or warnings for our coast. But long-range forecasts show the storm crossing Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula into the Gulf of Mexico, and Texas is among the places it could eventually go.

That makes this Labor Day weekend a good time to do the things we have been writing about all summer.

"It is too early to say where Rafael ends up," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Corpus Christi. "What we can say is that it's the peak of the season and the Gulf is warm. People should use the holiday weekend to get ready rather than wait for a cone."

What the bases are saying. There are no changes to operations at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. "We are watching the forecast, as we do with every storm," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station. "If anything changes for our sailors, civilians and families, they will hear it from their chain of command and from us."

What families can do this weekend:

Check the kit. Water, shelf-stable food, medicines, flashlights, batteries, a battery radio, cash and copies of important papers. Replace what the kids ate in July.

Know your zone. Look up your evacuation zone and decide now where you would go. If you would need a ride to evacuate, register with the county for evacuation assistance by calling 2-1-1.

Talk to your service member. Who secures the house if they are called in? Who takes the pets? Write it down.

Top off. Fill the gas tank and refill prescriptions before lines form, not after.

Find your people. Make sure your command's family readiness contact has your current phone number, and that you have theirs.

Forecasters said last month that they expected above-normal activity for the rest of the season. Rafael may or may not be our storm. Either way, a ready family has a better holiday weekend.

We will post updates as the forecast firms up. Enjoy the long weekend, and keep an eye on the weather.

item.title: September is here: Labor Day weekend plans, and the peak of hurricane season
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: A long weekend for many families is a good time to rest, travel safely and finish the hurricane plan. Plus: squadrons wrap a steady summer, and the depot keeps hiring.
item.content:encoded:
Happy September from all of us at Anchor & Rotor. For many families, this week means a long weekend, the first real routine of the school year and maybe one last trip to the beach. On the Coastal Bend, it also means the statistical peak of hurricane season.

Labor Day weekend first. Commands typically hold safety briefs before long weekends, and the advice never changes because it never stops being true: plan your drive, rest before you go, never drink and drive, wear a life jacket on the water and watch the kids in the surf. Expect heavy traffic to the islands and longer waits for the ferry.

On the airfield, NAS Corpus Christi's training squadrons wrapped a summer on a normal schedule, and the station completed a routine readiness inspection earlier in the season. Base services continue to operate normally. Across the field, Corpus Christi Army Depot is still hiring helicopter mechanics. If you know someone with the skills, point them to the federal job announcements.

Now the season. Forecasters expect above-normal Atlantic activity for the rest of hurricane season, and the weeks just ahead are traditionally the busiest. If you built your family plan with us last week, use the long weekend to finish it. If you did not, here is the short version.

Know your zone and your destination. Fill prescriptions. Keep the gas tank at least half full. Put IDs, orders and insurance papers in one waterproof folder. Update NFAAS if you are a Navy family, or check your unit's accountability process if you are Army or a depot civilian. If your household shares one car with a service member who could be at work when a storm comes, register for evacuation help by calling 2-1-1.

For families who arrived on new orders this summer: this is your first Coastal Bend hurricane season. Ask a neighbor who has been through one. They will have opinions, and most of them will be useful.

Enjoy the weekend. We will be back next week, and sooner if public affairs offices release guidance families need.

item.title: Your family hurricane plan, built for the season's busiest stretch
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Forecasters expect an above-normal rest of the season. Here is a plan built for military families, including what to do if your service member is at work when a storm comes.
item.content:encoded:
Every military family on the Coastal Bend has some version of the same story. The storm is coming, the kids need packing, the dog needs his pills, and the service member is at work, on duty or a thousand miles away. This week's column is for the person who ends up doing it alone.

Forecasters now expect above-normal Atlantic activity for the rest of the season, and the weeks from now into October are historically the busiest. That makes this the right week to finish your plan, not the week a storm has a name.

Plan for one adult. Assume the adult at home will handle an evacuation alone, because service members and many depot employees may have duties before and after a storm. Write the plan down so a teenager or a neighbor could follow it.

Get accounted for. Navy families should confirm their contact information in the Navy Family Accountability and Assessment System, NFAAS. Army families and depot civilians should ask their unit or supervisor how accountability works for them. After a storm, commands need to know you are safe, and they will look in those systems first.

Build the folder. ID cards, orders, powers of attorney, insurance policies, vehicle titles, medical records and a list of medications go in one waterproof folder. Take photos of everything and store them where you can reach them from any phone.

Know where you would go. Find out whether your home is in an evacuation zone. Pick a destination inland and a second choice. If your command issues evacuation guidance for families, follow it, and keep receipts for travel and lodging.

Short on cars? County emergency managers are urging residents without cars to register for evacuation help by calling 2-1-1. That includes households that share one vehicle with a service member who may be at work when the order comes.

Talk to the kids. Tell them the plan in plain words. Children handle a plan better than a surprise.

Base services are operating normally. We will share official guidance from public affairs offices as soon as it is released.

item.title: Depot keeps hiring helicopter mechanics; air station squadrons hold a steady summer pace
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Corpus Christi Army Depot's hiring push continues while training squadrons at NAS Corpus Christi keep a normal summer schedule. Plus a reminder for families: the busiest half of hurricane season is ahead.
item.content:encoded:
If you have spent any time in base housing or on the hangar floor this summer, you have probably heard about the depot's job openings before you saw them posted. Corpus Christi Army Depot is hiring helicopter mechanics, and word has traveled fast through spouse networks, neighborhood group chats and the commissary checkout line.

The depot, which sits on NAS Corpus Christi, is the Army's primary depot for rotary-wing maintenance, overhauling and repairing helicopters for units across the force. Its hiring this summer has focused on mechanics, and applicants are directed to federal job announcements on USAJOBS. Spouses with aviation maintenance experience may want to check whether they qualify for military spouse preference on those announcements.

Across the airfield, the training squadrons at NAS Corpus Christi are on a normal summer schedule. The station completed a routine readiness inspection earlier this summer, and base services are operating normally. For families who arrived during this summer's moving season, that means training aircraft overhead from morning into the evening. Most neighbors stop noticing after the first month.

Now the reminder. Hurricane season runs through November, and the weeks ahead are traditionally the busiest. County emergency managers have held preparedness fairs this summer and are urging residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance by calling 2-1-1. That applies to military families too, especially households that share one vehicle with a service member who may be on duty when a storm comes.

Navy families: make sure your information is current in the Navy Family Accountability and Assessment System, known as NFAAS. Army families and depot civilians: ask your supervisor or sponsor's unit how accountability works for your organization after an evacuation.

Keep copies of ID cards, orders, powers of attorney and insurance papers in one waterproof folder, and tell someone outside the area where it is.

Next week: building a family hurricane plan when one spouse may be at work, on duty or deployed when the call comes.

item.title: Back to school for base families: bus stops, busy gates and a storm plan in the backpack
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: The school year begins across Nueces County as districts review their storm closure plans. Three questions to ask your child's school, and one card to tuck in the lunchbox.
item.content:encoded:
School starts across Nueces County this week, and for military families that means new bus stops, new teachers and, for those who arrived this summer, a new district altogether. A few notes to make the first week easier.

Know your district's storm plan. As the year begins, local districts are reviewing their storm closure plans. Ask your child's school three questions: How will you tell me school is closed? Where do students go if a closure is called during the day? Who is allowed to pick up my child if I am on duty? Then make sure the school has a working phone number for you and for a backup adult. If your service member will be away this fall, update that list before they leave.

Put it in the backpack. A card with your phone numbers, a backup contact and your home address weighs nothing. Little ones forget numbers when they are scared. Tuck one in the backpack and one in the lunchbox.

Mornings near the gates. "Expect heavier traffic around the station in the mornings and when school lets out," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. "Give yourself a few extra minutes and watch for kids at the bus stops." Training squadrons remain on a normal schedule, he said.

Depot families. Corpus Christi Army Depot's hiring push continues, and many new hires are local parents. "A lot of our workforce is doing the school drop-off before they clock in, the same as everybody else," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot.

While you are filling out forms. The county is urging residents who would need a ride to evacuate to register for evacuation assistance now, not when a storm is on the map. If you know a neighbor without a car, perhaps a retiree down the street, pass that along.

The peak of hurricane season arrives about the same time as the first progress reports. A calm August is a gift. Use it.

Got a first-day-of-school photo? Send it to the Anchor & Rotor and we will share a few next week.

item.title: Editor's note: Don't let a calm summer fool you
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: The Coastal Bend has had a busy, sunny summer. That is exactly why base families should finish their hurricane prep now.
item.content:encoded:
This is an opinion column from the editor of Anchor & Rotor Weekly.

It has been a good summer around here. The flight line has been busy with training, the depot is hiring, the island businesses are booming and a lot of us have spent our weekends on the beach. When things are this calm, it is easy to push the hurricane checklist to next week.

I have been a Navy spouse long enough to know how that goes. Next week becomes next month, and then one day the store is out of water and you are standing in the bread aisle with a toddler on your hip, wondering why you didn't do this in August.

So here is my pitch, from one family to another. Relief agencies are already stocking their warehouses for the peak of the season. Do the same at home, a little at a time. Nueces County is still urging residents without cars to register for evacuation help through 2-1-1. If your spouse is away and you share one car, think hard about whether that means you. And know your evacuation zone, which depends on where you live, not where you work.

Talk to your kids about the plan in a calm voice, on a calm day. Put the important papers in one waterproof bag. Make sure your command knows how to reach you if you leave town, and that you know how to check in.

And look out for the new families. Moving season brings people who have never lived on a coast. Invite them over, share your list and show them which aisle the batteries are in.

None of this is about fear. It is about getting the boring part done while the sun is shining, so that if a storm ever does come, we can spend our energy on each other instead of on the bread aisle.

Done your prep? Send us your best tip, and we will share the good ones in a future issue.

item.title: New to the Coastal Bend? Moving season meets hurricane season
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: Families arriving on summer orders have a lot to unpack. Put a hurricane plan near the top of the box pile.
item.content:encoded:
Summer is moving season for military families, and the Coastal Bend is no exception. Moving trucks are pulling up to houses in Flour Bluff, Kingsville and Portland, and new arrivals are learning where the commissary is, which school their kids will attend and how hot August really gets.

There is one more thing to learn early: your hurricane plan.

Start with your county. Evacuation zones and orders come from local emergency managers, and they depend on where you live, not where you work. Families in Corpus Christi and Flour Bluff fall under Nueces County. Kingsville families should check with Kleberg County. Portland and Ingleside are in San Patricio County.

Nueces County has been holding preparedness fairs this summer and urging residents without cars to register for evacuation help through the state's 2-1-1 registry. "If you're new, come see us," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Learn your zone before you need it, and learn it from us, not from the internet."

On base, it is business as usual. NAS Corpus Christi completed a routine readiness inspection last week, and services are running normally. "Everything's open. If you're new, come by and get your bearings," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a station public affairs officer.

New-arrival checklist: Save your county emergency office's website and social media accounts. Sign up for local alerts. Learn your evacuation zone. Keep orders, IDs and records in a waterproof bag. If your household has one car and a spouse who may be away, line up a backup ride now. Introduce yourself to a neighbor. And find your command's family readiness contacts before you need them.

Welcome to the Coastal Bend. The beaches are great, the people are friendly and the summer is long. Get your plan done early, and enjoy the rest.

item.title: This week on base: inspection wrapped, services normal, and a brigade headed for the port
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: NAS Corpus Christi finished a routine readiness inspection with no change to services, and a Fort Hood aviation brigade will move equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer.
item.content:encoded:
A quick look at what is new around the installations this week.

Inspection complete: NAS Corpus Christi wrapped up a routine readiness inspection, and base services are operating normally. "Thank you to every sailor, civilian and contractor who put in the extra hours to get ready for it," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a station public affairs officer. "For families, nothing changes. Everything's open on its usual hours."

Brigade movement: An aviation brigade from Fort Hood will move its helicopters and equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer for an overseas rotation. "We'll be ready to deploy when the port is ready for us," Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer, said in announcing the move Wednesday.

What that means locally: The move runs through the port, not the air station, and the Army has not released dates or details. As always, Anchor & Rotor does not report unit movement details beyond what public affairs offices release. If you have a loved one in the brigade, your soldier's unit and family readiness group are the right sources for information.

Depot still hiring: Corpus Christi Army Depot continues to recruit helicopter mechanics. Veterans and military spouses with maintenance experience can find openings on USAJOBS.

Flight line: Training squadrons are flying their normal summer schedule. Expect turboprops over Flour Bluff on weekday mornings.

Hurricane season reminder: Nueces County preparedness fairs continue this summer. If your household will not have a car in an evacuation, register through the state registry by dialing 2-1-1, and make sure your command knows how to reach you if you leave town.

Have news from your squadron, shop or family group? Send it our way for a future issue.

item.title: Hurricane season starts at the kitchen table: a checklist for base families
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: County preparedness fairs are open to everyone, including military households. Here is what to do now, plus news from the depot's hiring push.
item.content:encoded:
If your family moved to the Coastal Bend this year, welcome. You picked a beautiful place, and you arrived in hurricane season. The good news is that most of the work of getting ready happens at your own kitchen table, long before anyone is watching a forecast.

Nueces County emergency managers are holding hurricane-season preparedness fairs this summer, and military families are welcome. The county's message is simple: know your evacuation zone, build a kit, and if you will not have a vehicle, register for evacuation help now through the state's 2-1-1 registry.

"Military families are our neighbors, and the same advice applies: know your zone and have a plan to leave," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If you won't have a car, tell us now, not when the wind is blowing."

That last point matters more than many families expect. A household with one car and a spouse away on duty can find itself without a ride on the day it counts. Make a plan with a neighbor, a friend from your command's family readiness group, or the county registry.

Your kitchen-table checklist: Look up your evacuation zone and save it in your phone. Keep copies of orders, IDs, insurance papers and medical records in a waterproof bag. Stock water, nonperishable food, medications, chargers and pet supplies. Know how your command will account for you and how to check in if you leave the area. Pick a meeting place and an out-of-town contact.

Depot hiring: Corpus Christi Army Depot is recruiting helicopter mechanics. "Veterans and military spouses bring exactly the kind of discipline this work needs," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a depot public affairs specialist. Openings are posted on USAJOBS.

Flight line: Training squadrons at NAS Corpus Christi are flying a normal summer schedule, so expect the usual sound of turboprops over Flour Bluff.

item.title: Welcome to summer on the bases: depot hiring, steady flying and a hot July
item.dc:creator: Carla Benavides
item.description: New to the Coastal Bend on orders? Here is what the public affairs offices are sharing this week, plus a few tips for the heat.
item.content:encoded:
If you just moved here on orders, welcome to the Coastal Bend in July. It is hot, the islands are packed, and the bases are settling into the steady rhythm of summer. Here is what the public affairs offices are sharing this week.

Depot hiring. Corpus Christi Army Depot is hiring helicopter mechanics. "We're looking for people who like to fix things and want to stay in this community," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a public affairs specialist for the depot. "Veterans and military spouses with maintenance experience should take a look. So should people who grew up down the road." Job announcements are posted on the federal jobs site, she said, and applicants should read the documents list before they apply.

Flying schedule. The training squadrons at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi are on a normal summer schedule. "Student aviators are flying, the weather has cooperated, and it's a routine summer," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the air station. Families new to base housing or nearby neighborhoods will hear training aircraft during the day. That is the sound of the station doing its job.

Heat and water. The city is asking residents to conserve water while the heat holds. For base families that means watering early or late, fixing the dripping hose bib and keeping an eye on kids and pets in the afternoon. Drink water before you feel thirsty, and never leave a child or a pet in a parked car, not even for a minute.

Beach traffic. Tourism is heavy on Mustang and Padre islands this month. If you are headed out for a beach day, leave early, pack shade and expect a slow drive home.

One more thing for newcomers: hurricane season runs through November. A quiet stretch is the right time to learn your evacuation zone and start a kit. We will have more on that in the coming weeks.

New in town and not sure where to start? Stop by your installation's family support office, and send your questions to the Anchor & Rotor. We answer them.
